content: The Rome Process is an international initiative aimed at defining and categorizing functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGIDs), which are conditions of unknown cause, such as Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and Functional Dyspepsia. This approach represents a significant shift in medical thinking, as it moves away from relying solely on structural or biochemical evidence for diagnosis. Instead, it adopts a methodology similar to that used in psychiatry for classifying and diagnosing psychiatric disorders, as seen in the DSM-IV criteria. Importantly, these diagnoses are not meant to be diagnoses of exclusion but require a more proactive and positive diagnostic approach. Historically, systematic efforts to classify FGIDs began as early as 1962, when Chaudhary and Truelove published a retrospective review of IBS patients in Oxford, England. In 1978, the Manning Criteria for IBS were introduced, marking a pivotal moment in the classification of FGIDs. This led to increased scientific interest and research in the field. The Rome criteria have evolved over time, starting with the Rome Guidelines for IBS in 1989, followed by the Rome I Classification System for FGIDs in 1990, the Rome I Criteria for IBS in 1992, and subsequent updates in 1994, 1999 (Rome II), and 2006 (Rome III). The Rome II and III criteria also incorporated pediatric guidelines into the consensus. The Rome criteria are developed through a consensus process using the Delphi method, organized by the Rome Coordinating Committee. This process involves extensive collaboration among investigators, who work in committees over several months via mail and telephone conferences, culminating in a defining meeting held in Rome, Italy. The Rome III effort included 87 participants from 18 countries, with representation from non-Western nations such as China, Brazil, Chile, Venezuela, Hungary, and Romania. Additional working teams addressed issues like gender, societal, patient, and social factors, as well as pharmacology and pharmacokinetics. For pediatric FGIDs, two committees (neonate/toddler and child/adolescent) were established. In the Rome III classification, FGIDs in adults are divided into six major domains: esophageal (Category A), gastroduodenal (Category B), bowel (Category C), functional abdominal pain syndrome (Category D), biliary (Category E), and anorectal (Category F). Functional bowel disorders (Category C) include IBS (C1), functional bloating (C2), functional constipation (C3), and functional diarrhea (C4). IBS (C1) is specifically defined as abdominal pain associated with changes in bowel habits, distinct from functional diarrhea. For pediatric patients, FGIDs are classified by age range and symptom patterns or areas of symptoms. Neonate/toddler disorders (Category G) include infant regurgitation (G1), infant rumination syndrome (G2), cyclic vomiting syndrome (G3), infant colic (G4), functional diarrhea (G5), infant dyschezia (G6), and functional constipation (G7). Child/adolescent disorders (Category H) include vomiting and aerophagia (H1), abdominal pain-related FGIDs (H2), and constipation and incontinence (H3). Each category contains specific disorders with distinct clinical features. The Rome Process for diagnosing IBS involves a combination of clinical evaluation, laboratory testing, and the application of diagnostic criteria. Abdominal pain is the cardinal symptom required for an IBS diagnosis. The Rome II criteria, and more recently the Rome III criteria, are used to diagnose IBS after a thorough review of the patient’s medical history and physical examination, ensuring no red flag symptoms are present. According to the Rome II committees and the Functional Brain-Gut Research Group, IBS can be diagnosed if, over the preceding 12 months, the patient experienced at least 12 weeks (not necessarily consecutive) of abdominal discomfort or pain with at least two of the following features: relief with defecation, onset associated with a change in stool frequency, or onset associated with a change in stool form (appearance). Additional symptoms supporting an IBS diagnosis include abnormal stool frequency (more than three bowel movements per day or fewer than three per week), abnormal stool form (lumpy/hard or loose/watery stools), abnormal stool passage (straining, urgency, or a feeling of incomplete evacuation), and bloating or a sensation of abdominal distension. Supportive symptoms also include passing mucus during bowel movements and sensations of abdominal fullness or swelling. IBS subtypes are categorized as diarrhea-predominant or constipation-predominant based on specific symptom patterns. However, the validity and stability of these subtypes over time remain uncertain and require further research. Due to the variability and heterogeneity of IBS symptoms, the terms IBS with constipation and IBS with diarrhea are preferred over constipation-predominant and diarrhea-predominant IBS. This variability also poses challenges for clinical trials and drug therapy. The Rome criteria are not intended as management guidelines but serve as the gold standard for diagnosing IBS. Diagnostic accuracy exceeds 95% when the Rome II criteria are met, the patient’s history and physical examination do not suggest other causes, and initial laboratory tests are negative. While IBS was historically considered a diagnosis of exclusion, it is now diagnosed based on meeting the Rome inclusion criteria (updated by Rome III) and ruling out other conditions through history, physical examination, and laboratory testing. However, an IBS diagnosis in adults is often only a starting point, requiring further investigation to identify any treatable underlying conditions.
